newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Ringgit falls sharply on dollar strength, demand.
newsitem.headline: Ringgit falls sharply on dollar strength, demand.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit hit a five-month low on Thursday afternoon following an overnight fall triggered by the U.S. dollar's recovery against major currencies, dealers and analysts said.
At 1051 GMT, the ringgit was at 2.5074/79 per dollar against 2.5013/20 at close of the Kuala Lumpur market on Wednesday. It hit a low of 2.5080.

While the fall would immediately be capped at the next support level of 2.5100 to the dollar, pressure would continue on the ringgit on month-end demand for U.S. unit from Malaysian corporations, the dealers and analysts said.
Dealers said the ringgit's decline was aided by the commercial demand from Kuala Lumpur and a large speculative sale from Hong Kong.
"It started with some stop-loss sales caused by the dollar's rise. Then there was a big ringgit sale by a Hong Kong party," said a dealer with a U.S. bank in Singapore.
Dealers said the U.S. dollar rallied strongly against major currencies starting on Wednesday, despite a disappointment over the absence of a U.S. interest rate rise on Tuesday.
The market had widely expected the Federal Open Market Committee to raise interest rates by 25 basis points.
Dealers said two Malaysian statements aided the decline of the ringgit.
One was from Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad who said in New York he believed in the need for a "competitive exchange rate" that reflects what he called "long-term market forces".
Dealers quoted Mahathir as reaffirming that central bank intervention in foreign exchange market would be limited to smoothing out sharp short-term fluctuations.

In another comment, the central bank Bank Negara Deputy Governor, Fong Weng Phak, said on Thursday that Malaysia does not expect a major improvement in its services account deficit this year, though the trade gap has improved sharply in the first seven months.
Malaysia's trade deficit in the first seven months of the year fell to 1.4 billion ringgit from 6.9 billion in the same period of 1995.
The Government has forecast a current account deficit of 17.0 billion ringgit against 17.8 billion last year.
Analysts had last year said the high current account deficit was causing overheating in the fast-growing Malaysian economy.
"I don't think the services account can improve that dramatically in a year," he told reporters at a conference on human resources in the financial services industry.
"But, the (overall) current account would improve," he said, but did not give details.
Analysts said there was no fundamental reason for the sharp decline of the ringgit.
"In fact, the fundamentals have really been improving," said Sim Moh Siong, economist with Citibank in Singapore.

He said the ringgit exchange rate has been used as a tool to curb domestic inflation. "It has worked very well. Its appreciation has helped slow down the economy and the impact on the trade has not been negative," he said.
He said the market may have been taking positions in anticipation of the tight monetary policy being eased after the positive trade data announcement.
"But the market may have overlooked that there is need for a tight monetary policy. There is also room for fiscal restraint in the October annual budget," Sim said.
"My view is that the reaction (to ringgit) is not justified because fundamentally nothing has changed," he said.
